clue.text: Exhausted, in Graham Greene's case

definitions.meaning: worn out, with no energy or enthusiasm left
Graham Greene wrote the 1960 novel A ... Case, so this describes the condition in his title

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that the novelist Graham Greene was worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition borrows the title of Greene's novel A Burnt-Out Case: 'case' looks like 'as for Greene', but it is the last word of his title.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone exhausted by overwork is spent, a state of utter fatigue, which is also the condition of the leper colony doctor in Greene's book.

clue.text: Queen Victoria claimed she was

parts.note: points to the famous remark attributed to Queen Victoria, 'We are not amused', so the clue asks what state she declared herself in

explanation.definitionFit: Victoria's reputed rebuke 'We are not amused' declares her displeased, so she claimed to be in a state of not being entertained.

clue.text: Group of musicians without a goal, presumably?

parts.note: no means without, as in 'no money'
the net is the goal in football or hockey

explanation.surface: A band with no goal in life, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the comic reading: a goalless team might be said to have 'no net'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is an ensemble of nine players, a kind of musical group.

clue.text: Editor, one immersed in work on multifaceted emotional issue

indicators.note: something immersed in a liquid is surrounded by it, so the next pieces go inside the word for work

parts.note: an opus is a musical or literary work
I is the Roman numeral for one
complex means having many parts or facets

explanation.surface: An editor absorbed in a book about some many-sided psychological problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'immersed in' signals the container; 'on' is only a link joining the two words of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Freud's term names a child's unconscious desire for the opposite-sex parent, a psychological problem of feeling.

clue.text: Block old savings scheme with sovereign invested

indicators.note: money invested is put into something, so the monarch's letters go inside the savings scheme

parts.note: TESSA was the Tax-Exempt Special Savings Account, a UK savings product of the 1990s
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the sovereign

explanation.surface: Someone blocks an old savings plan in which a monarch has put money.
explanation.walkthrough: The old scheme was a British tax-free savings account, replaced by the ISA in 1999; 'invested' signals the monarch going inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tessera is a small square tile or cube used in mosaic, a little block of stone or glass.

clue.text: Indian island discovered after short journey

parts.note: a hop is a short trip, as in 'a quick hop across the Channel'

explanation.surface: An Indian island found at the end of a brief trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' means a Native American here: the Hopi are a people of Arizona. 'discovered after' joins the island letter to the end of HOP.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hopi are a Native American people of northeastern Arizona, and so American Indians.

clue.text: Midlands town audibly welcomes Welshman

indicators.note: says that the words before it are to be heard rather than spelt, as if spoken out loud

parts.note: to hail someone is to welcome them, and Owen is a typical Welsh name

explanation.surface: A Midlands town loudly greets a man from Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: HAILS OWEN, spoken, sounds like the town; Halesowen is near Birmingham in the West Midlands of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Halesowen is a market town in the West Midlands county of England.

clue.text: Basil, for example, endlessly upset

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter of the phrase for basil is dropped

parts.note: basil is a pot herb, a herb grown for the kitchen

explanation.surface: Someone called Basil is endlessly troubled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basil' looks like a man's name but is the kitchen herb. 'upset' is a noun here: a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: A pother is a commotion or fuss, and an upset in the sense of a disturbance.

clue.text: Concluding part of White Fang, a thriller surprisingly prominent?

indicators.note: something done surprisingly is unexpected, telling us to rearrange the letters gathered here
the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of 'White' is used

explanation.surface: A remark on the ending of Jack London's novel White Fang being an unexpectedly exciting read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' shuffles E (the end of 'White') with FANG A THRILLER, fourteen letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who seems bigger than real life stands out, being conspicuous or flamboyant.

clue.text: Corrupt warden given a caution

indicators.note: to corrupt something is to alter it from its true form, so the following word's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dishonest prison warden receives a caution.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone given a caution has been admonished, told off with a threat of what follows next time.

clue.text: It may grow in English allotments

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters across the two words that follow

explanation.surface: Some plant may be raised in English allotment gardens.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits within 'Englis(H ALLOT)ments'. An allotment is a small rented plot for growing vegetables in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallot is a small onion-like bulb that gardeners raise, so it is one thing that may grow.

clue.text: Untidy mess in most of fish shop

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another, here the mess inside the shortened fish
most of a word is all but its last letter, so the fish loses its tail

parts.note: the mullet is a fish
a tip is British slang for a very untidy place: 'his room is a tip'

explanation.surface: A fishmonger's shop is a chaotic mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fish shop' reads as one thing, but 'fish' is wordplay and 'shop' is the definition. MULLE (most of MULLET) has TIP put in.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a multiple is a chain store, a retailer with many branches.

clue.text: Woman's brought in fuel cuts

indicators.note: something brought into a place ends up inside it, so the woman's word goes inside the fuel

parts.note: gas is a fuel
she is the pronoun for a woman; the 's stands for 'has'

explanation.surface: A woman has brought in fuel cuts, such as a rationing order.
explanation.definitionFit: Gashes are deep wounds made with a blade, so long cuts in the skin.

annotationWithheld.clue: Songster gradually moves close to piano in

clue.text: Rabbit and classy wine served up by British eatery

parts.note: to rabbit or gas is British slang for chattering on

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the words are read from the bottom upwards, so in reverse

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in U and non-U
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Rabbit with a smart wine, served by a British restaurant, sounds like a gastropub menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' looks like the dish but is chatter (rabbit and gas both mean talk idly). 'served up' turns U PORT to TROPU.
explanation.definitionFit: A gastropub is a pub serving good food, so a place to dine.

clue.text: Clear ice off vegetable

indicators.note: something off has gone bad or wrong, so the two words are scrambled

explanation.surface: Instructions to wipe the ice off a vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Celeriac is a root vegetable, a variety of celery grown for its knobbly bulb.

clue.text: Ex-cabinet member, caught and severely 3 punished, is treated unfairly

parts.note: Clare Short was a British Labour Cabinet minister who resigned in 2003
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
hanged means put to death, severely punished

explanation.surface: A former minister is caught and harshly punished: hardly fair treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare Short was International Development Secretary under Tony Blair. 'severely' qualifies the punishment, which is hanging.
explanation.definitionFit: To be cheated, especially by being given too little money in change, is to be dealt with unjustly.

clue.text: Spicy sauce, important element mostly in Mexican food

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another, here the shortened element inside the food

parts.note: a taco is a folded Mexican tortilla

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter

parts.note: the base is the main or fundamental element of something

explanation.surface: Hot sauce is a key ingredient in Mexican cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'important element' means the basis or foundation; 'mostly' drops its last letter before it goes inside the food.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabasco is a hot pepper sauce, a fiery condiment from Louisiana.

clue.text: Famous horror film featuring bear, we hear?

indicators.note: means the word just before it is to be heard rather than read, so its sound gives the answer

parts.note: to bear something is to carry it

explanation.surface: A notorious horror film starring a bear, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear' looks like the animal but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Carrie is Brian De Palma's 1976 film of the Stephen King novel, a classic of the horror genre.

clue.text: Governor's role, when 4 circulating

indicators.note: going round, so the letters for role and when are turned back to front

parts.note: a part is a role in a play
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A governor's job, when it is going the rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The '4' in the clue as held is a stray cross-reference figure and gives no letters; 'circulating' turns the whole two-word run round.
explanation.definitionFit: A satrap was a provincial governor in ancient Persia, and now any petty ruler.

clue.text: Dad began trembling, having dressed wounds

indicators.note: something trembling is shaken, so the letters of the two words are mixed up

explanation.surface: A father shook after tending someone's wounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandaged person has had their injuries wrapped, covered with strips of cloth.

clue.text: Temper rising during pregnancy?

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read from bottom to top, so in reverse
something during a period falls within it, so the answer lies inside the next word

explanation.surface: A tendency to lose one's temper while expecting a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'p(REGNA)ncy' backwards: 'during' hides the letters, 'rising' turns them.
explanation.definitionFit: Temper in the sense of a fit of rage means fury.

clue.text: Subdue crowd backing leaders of rebellion

indicators.note: the leading letters of a word come at its front

parts.note: to press round is to crowd, and a press is a crowd

explanation.surface: Putting down a mob that supports the ringleaders of a revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' means supporting from behind, so the crowd comes after the first two letters of 'rebellion'.
explanation.definitionFit: To repress is to hold down or quell, so to subdue.

clue.text: Girl on bike, back to front

indicators.note: part of the word is moved from the front to the back

parts.note: riding means on a bike

explanation.surface: A girl on a bicycle, sitting the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to front' moves the first three letters, RID, to the end of RIDING.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingrid is a woman's given name, as in Ingrid Bergman.

clue.text: European taking time off in French port, going west

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means read from right to left
the letter for time is removed from the port
the letter for time is removed from the port

parts.note: Brest is a port in Brittany

explanation.surface: A European visitor takes time off in a French port before heading west.
explanation.walkthrough: BREST without T is BRES; 'going west' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A Serb is a person from Serbia, a country of Europe.

clue.text: Concerned with a particular subject — the monorail?

definitions.meaning: a mind obsessed with a single topic is said to be like this
a monorail runs on a single rail, so it literally has only one line

explanation.surface: Someone obsessed with one topic is compared to a monorail.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-track mind is narrowly fixated, while a monorail literally has a single line.
